subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 63-year-old man is hospitalized with an acute inferior STEMI. On hospital day 4 he suddenly develops severe dyspnea and hypotension. A new holosystolic murmur is heard at the apex radiating to the axilla, and chest x-ray shows severe pulmonary edema. Emergent echocardiography is ordered.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_correct: Papillary muscle rupture occurs 2–7 days after myocardial infarction and can result in acute mitral regurgitation, causing cardiogenic shock and severe pulmonary edema — matching this patient's day-4 collapse with a new apical holosystolic murmur radiating to the axilla. Posteromedial papillary muscle rupture is much more common than anterolateral, because the posteromedial muscle has a single artery blood supply (the posterior descending artery), consistent with his inferior infarct.

explanation_incorrect.A: Ventricular free wall rupture occurs 5–14 days post-MI and causes cardiac tamponade or internal hemorrhage, often fatal — not a new apical regurgitant murmur.
explanation_incorrect.C: Interventricular septal rupture (3–5 days) produces a ventricular septal defect with a left-to-right shunt, a holosystolic murmur at the left sternal border, and increased O2 saturation in the right ventricle.
explanation_incorrect.D: Postcardiac injury (Dressler) syndrome occurs weeks to several months post-MI as an autoimmune pericarditis, presenting with pleuritic pain and a friction rub.
explanation_incorrect.E: Peri-infarction pericarditis occurs 1–3 days post-MI with pleuritic chest pain, a pericardial friction rub, and a small effusion, and is usually self-limited.

educationalObjective: Papillary muscle rupture (2–7 days post-MI) causes acute mitral regurgitation with cardiogenic shock and pulmonary edema; the posteromedial papillary muscle is far more vulnerable due to its single PDA supply.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 70-year-old woman with an anterior STEMI develops cardiogenic shock on hospital day 4. A new harsh holosystolic murmur is heard at the left sternal border. Right heart catheterization shows a step-up in oxygen saturation from the right atrium to the right ventricle, along with elevated right ventricular pressure. Pulmonary edema is present on chest imaging.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_correct: Interventricular septal rupture occurs 3–5 days after myocardial infarction when macrophage-mediated degradation of the necrotic septum creates a ventricular septal defect. The resulting left-to-right shunt increases O2 saturation and pressure in the right ventricle — the catheterization step-up from right atrium to right ventricle is the hallmark. Symptoms can range from mild to severe with cardiogenic shock and pulmonary edema, as in this patient.

explanation_incorrect.A: Papillary muscle rupture causes acute mitral regurgitation with an apical holosystolic murmur and pulmonary edema, but it does not create an oxygen saturation step-up in the right ventricle.
explanation_incorrect.B: Ventricular free wall rupture (5–14 days) leads to cardiac tamponade or internal hemorrhage and is often fatal; it does not produce a left-to-right shunt.
explanation_incorrect.C: Ventricular pseudoaneurysm (3–14 days) is a contained free wall rupture without endocardium or myocardium, with mural thrombus embolus risk and possible rupture into tamponade — no intracardiac shunt step-up.
explanation_incorrect.D: Peri-infarction pericarditis occurs 1–3 days post-MI with pleuritic pain, a friction rub, and a small effusion; it causes no murmur or shunt.

educationalObjective: Interventricular septal rupture (3–5 days post-MI) from macrophage-mediated degradation creates a VSD with an oxygen saturation step-up in the right ventricle and raised RV pressure.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 68-year-old man is in the hospital 10 days after a large lateral myocardial infarction when he suddenly becomes severely hypotensive. He is diaphoretic with a heart rate of 118/min, distended neck veins, and distant, muffled heart sounds. Echocardiography shows a large pericardial effusion with right ventricular diastolic collapse.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_correct: Ventricular free wall rupture occurs 5–14 days after myocardial infarction and leads to cardiac tamponade or internal hemorrhage, often fatal. This patient's day-10 collapse with hypotension, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds, and an effusion with diastolic collapse is tamponade from free wall rupture. Notably, LV hypertrophy and previous MI protect against free wall rupture.

explanation_incorrect.A: A true ventricular aneurysm appears 2 weeks to several months post-MI as an outward bulge with dyskinesia and fibrosis, associated with mural thrombus — it does not cause acute tamponade.
explanation_incorrect.B: Interventricular septal rupture (3–5 days) creates a VSD with a left-to-right shunt, left sternal border murmur, and RV oxygen step-up — not tamponade physiology.
explanation_incorrect.D: Papillary muscle rupture (2–7 days) causes acute mitral regurgitation with cardiogenic shock and severe pulmonary edema, not pericardial tamponade.
explanation_incorrect.E: Postcardiac injury (Dressler) syndrome occurs weeks to months after injury as an autoimmune pericarditis with pleuritic pain and friction rub.

educationalObjective: Ventricular free wall rupture (5–14 days post-MI) causes cardiac tamponade or internal hemorrhage and is often fatal; LV hypertrophy and previous MI are protective.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: During a cardiac pathology conference, an attending reviews autopsy specimens from patients who died of mechanical complications of myocardial infarction. He notes that rupture of the posteromedial papillary muscle is far more frequent than rupture of the anterolateral papillary muscle and asks the group to explain why.
question: Which of the following best explains the greater vulnerability of the posteromedial papillary muscle to rupture after myocardial infarction?

options.text: It has a single artery blood supply (posterior descending artery), whereas the anterolateral papillary muscle has a dual supply (LAD, LCX)
It has a dual supply from the LAD and LCX, whereas the anterolateral papillary muscle has a single supply
It is supplied exclusively by the left circumflex artery
It is perfused at substantially lower diastolic pressures than the anterolateral papillary muscle
It is directly exposed to higher left ventricular pressures than the anterolateral papillary muscle

explanation_correct: Posteromedial papillary muscle rupture is much more common than anterolateral papillary muscle rupture after myocardial infarction because the posteromedial muscle receives its blood supply from a single artery — the posterior descending artery — whereas the anterolateral papillary muscle has a dual supply from the LAD and the LCX. A single supply means one occluded vessel can devascularize the entire muscle.

explanation_incorrect.B: This reverses the supply patterns: it is the anterolateral papillary muscle that has the dual (LAD, LCX) supply, and the posteromedial muscle that has the single PDA supply.
explanation_incorrect.C: The posteromedial papillary muscle is supplied by the posterior descending artery, not exclusively by the left circumflex artery.
explanation_incorrect.D: Rupture susceptibility is explained by the arterial supply pattern, not by a difference in diastolic perfusion pressure between the two muscles.
explanation_incorrect.E: Both papillary muscles experience left ventricular pressures; the differing rupture rates reflect single versus dual arterial supply.

educationalObjective: The posteromedial papillary muscle ruptures more often post-MI because it depends on a single artery (the PDA), while the anterolateral muscle has a dual LAD + LCX supply.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 59-year-old man presents 8 days after an acute myocardial infarction with exertional dyspnea and a syncopal episode. Transthoracic echocardiography reveals a large outpouching arising from the lateral left ventricular wall, containing laminated thrombus. The cardiologist notes that this structure does not contain endocardium or myocardium.
question: Which of the following best characterizes this patient's complication?

options.text: It contains endocardium and myocardium and appears as an outward bulge with dyskinesia and fibrosis
It is less likely to rupture than a true ventricular aneurysm
It typically develops 2 weeks to several months after infarction
It is a free wall rupture contained by adherent pericardium or scar tissue, and is more likely to rupture than a true aneurysm
It arises from macrophage-mediated degradation of the interventricular septum

explanation_correct: This patient has a ventricular pseudoaneurysm, which occurs 3–14 days post-MI and represents a ventricular free wall rupture contained by adherent pericardium or scar tissue; it does not contain endocardium or myocardium. It may be asymptomatic or cause chest pain, murmur, arrhythmia, syncope, heart failure, or embolus from mural thrombus, and rupture leads to cardiac tamponade. Critically, a pseudoaneurysm is more likely to rupture than a true aneurysm.

explanation_incorrect.A: This describes a true ventricular aneurysm, which contains the ventricular wall layers and appears 2 weeks to several months post-MI as an outward bulge with dyskinesia and fibrosis; the pseudoaneurysm lacks endocardium and myocardium.
explanation_incorrect.B: The relationship is reversed: a pseudoaneurysm is more likely to rupture than a true aneurysm.
explanation_incorrect.C: A pseudoaneurysm occurs 3–14 days after infarction; the 2-weeks-to-several-months timeframe describes a true ventricular aneurysm.
explanation_incorrect.E: Macrophage-mediated degradation of the interventricular septum produces septal rupture with a ventricular septal defect, not a contained free wall outpouching.

educationalObjective: A ventricular pseudoaneurysm (3–14 days post-MI) is a contained free wall rupture lacking endocardium and myocardium, carries mural thrombus embolus risk, and is more likely to rupture than a true aneurysm.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 57-year-old woman presents 6 weeks after an anterior myocardial infarction with low-grade fever, malaise, and pleuritic chest pain. On examination there is a pericardial friction rub. ECG shows diffuse ST-segment elevations, and echocardiography reveals a small pericardial effusion. Her physician explains that her immune system is reacting against antigens released by her injured heart.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_correct: This is postcardiac injury syndrome, also called Dressler syndrome — pericarditis occurring weeks to several months after myocardial infarction due to an autoimmune reaction. Cardiac antigens released after injury lead to deposition of immune complexes in the pericardium, causing inflammation; the presentation includes pleuritic chest pain and a pericardial friction rub.

explanation_incorrect.A: Peri-infarction pericarditis occurs 1–3 days after infarction and is usually self-limited; this patient's presentation is 6 weeks out, in the Dressler window.
explanation_incorrect.C: Recurrent infarction would present with ischemic chest pain and ECG changes in a coronary distribution, not diffuse pericarditic ST elevations with a friction rub 6 weeks later.
explanation_incorrect.D: Papillary muscle rupture occurs 2–7 days post-MI and causes acute mitral regurgitation with cardiogenic shock and pulmonary edema.
explanation_incorrect.E: Ventricular free wall rupture occurs 5–14 days post-MI and causes cardiac tamponade or internal hemorrhage, often fatal — not an autoimmune pericarditis.

educationalObjective: Dressler (postcardiac injury) syndrome is an autoimmune pericarditis weeks to months after MI, caused by immune complex deposition in the pericardium from released cardiac antigens.
